1780824: On landing, wind gust blew plane off [centerline], Added full power for go-around and plane continued to turn from the runway. All airspeed lost and plane dropped (maybe 5-10 feet). One landing gear sheared off and plane went into grass to south of runway and other landing gear and wing broke. Pilot some minor scratches. Passenger no injury. Walked away from the plane.
1780834: Flying direct to ZZZ I had an iPad drop off the side window and I bent down to pick it up. Unfortunately the screen cracked and I attempted to assess the damage as well as re-mount it to the window. As I did this, the aircraft (no autopilot) inadvertently descended into a cloud layer I'd had intentions of passing over (I was within VFR mins above it) and suddenly I was IMC. I had mountainous terrain below, so I couldn't immediately descend, I tried climbing back to 10,500 feet, but at that point was still in the cloud. The airplane being a single engine piston I didn't have extra power to climb much higher so I watched my map closely to ensure I was moving past terrain, then began a descent. I advised ATC because I wanted to be sure I was heard in case something happened (ATC can't talk with me where I was due to rad and radio limitations from terrain). I descended and noticed my windscreen was icing up, and the wings began accumulate icing also. I continued descent until under the cloud layer and was able to safely land aircraft without incident.
1780845: Upon departing ZZZ to the south southeast for skydiving operations, I leveled the aircraft to maintain vertical separation from a cloud layer. After leveling the aircraft, I proceeded in the same direction towards an area of no cloud cover. I believe leveling/increasing speed of the aircraft while having the passenger window open in the cockpit, created unequal pressure and caused the sliding door to implode. I immediately reduced speed and began to change direction back towards ZZZ. The imploded door then exited the aircraft, striking the horizontal stabilizer and fell to the surface in pieces into what appeared to be a wooded area. After landing safely I proceeded to scout the area where the debris landed in another airplane. No debris, damage, gatherings or any activity regarding the incident were observed.
1780849: When flying a return leg from VIH at cruise altitude 9,000 feet, I encountered greater headwinds than were either forecast or anticipated. Winds aloft and ceiling/visibility forecasts were wildly off from what was predicted. On the initial flight of the morning from ZZZ to VIH I experienced a 10 kt. headwind for the duration of the flight. I planned fuel based on calm winds for the return leg with forecasts predicting a tailwind. Per my calculations I would return with 1.5 hours of fuel. In cruise on the return leg, a 5-8 kt. headwind was experienced, reducing the fuel reserve down to one hour at destination. Weather was not as forecast at the destination with visibility and ceilings dropping at the first stop. I attempted an RNAV approach which resulted in a missed approach. When I checked on with approach control the ceilings and visibility there were 400 ft. -4sm visibility. Once at the IAF it had dropped to 200 ft. and 1.5 miles of visibility and rapidly deteriorating. After the missed approach I had 48 minutes of fuel on board. I alerted ATC by saying I had 'Minimum Fuel' at which point they gave me priority vectors for ILS at the alternate. The approach was to minimums, but with the high intensity rabbit lights it was a successful approach and I made a full stop landing with 32 minutes of fuel. Factors were Fatigue/Hypoxia from a 6 hour flying day, my radio working as not as succinctly as it should have been, and impulsivity - trying to return home before dark to increase the odds of the approach being successful. I should have obtained more fuel at the prior airport despite my calculations of 1.5 hours after the return.
1780850: On Date, I planned a flight to land at 23M Clarke County (a non towered field), then on to ZZZ. I obtained a full flight briefing through Foreflight prior to departure and confirmed that the only airport NOTAM for 23M was that the PAPI for runway 34 was unusable. I departed and had an uneventful flight en route to 23M. About 6 miles from 23M, I announced my position and intention to land on runway 16 on the CTAF. I made position reports again on turning left downwind, left base, and final. Abeam the numbers on downwind leg, I reduced throttle to normal MAP for landing. As I turned from base to final, I went to reduce throttle to idle, but the throttle stuck at about 12 inches MAP. As I approached the runway, I tried very diligently to get the throttle unstuck by turning the throttle tension knob and firmly pulling on the throttle. I was able to get the throttle to pull back to idle just before crossing the runway threshold and proceeded to land on runway 16 at 23M. Once on the ground, a voice came over the radio that said 'You can't land here, the airport is closed, didn't you see the yellow X on the runway?' I had not seen any X's on the runway on approach. At this point I reached the entry to the taxiway and saw that it was blocked off. I responded that I was having a semi-emergency and was troubleshooting a stuck throttle. They asked if there was anything they could do to help. I replied no and that I think I had the problem resolved and would immediately back taxi and take back off. I told them I checked NOTAMs before I departed and that I hadn't seen any NOTAMS about a closure, to which they replied 'Well I don't know how that happened.' He stated that they had no fuel and something about that being why the airport was closed, which did not completely make sense to me at the time. I cycled the throttle several times to ensure it was not sticking and the engine responded properly. There were no obstructions on the runway that would prevent takeoff and there were no workers visible around the runway. As I taxied back to the takeoff end of runway 16, I was thinking about how I did not see any X's on the runway and how there was no NOTAM for the airport being closed when I did my briefing just an hour or so prior. I felt like a real bonehead for missing this. When I got to the end of the runway, I saw that there was in fact NO X ON THE PAVED RUNWAY INDICATING IT WAS CLOSED. There was a yellow X laying on the grass leading up to the runway threshold, but there were no markings on the runway itself. I departed without issue and returned to my home airport. I checked the NOTAMs for the airport again and confirmed that there were no NOTAMs for 23M being closed on this date. Three issues stand out to me in this situation. First, if a runway is to be closed, the yellow X needs to be ON the runway, not in the grass leading up to the runway. All examples of runway closure markings I have ever seen have been ON the runway surface. Second, if an airport or runway is to be temporarily closed, there should be a NOTAM for that closure. Third, while there was an X on the grass leading up to the runway, I did not see it on final approach due to being preoccupied troubleshooting the stuck throttle. In the future, I will do a more thorough job of looking AROUND the runway for yellow X's while on downwind leg and on final approach. I am not sure if an unauthorized individual may have placed the X's in the grass and the airport wasn't really officially closed. The person on the CTAF did not identify themselves so I do not know if they were airport officials or someone else. The lack of a NOTAM and improper placement of the X's leads me to think this may not have been an official airport closure. Nevertheless, I will do a better job of scanning the area around the runway from now on for any indication of problems.
1780859: The flight where this incident happened was a night VFR cross-country from ZZZ to ZZZ, as the final leg of a cross country flight along the route of ZZZ-ZZZ1-ZZZ2-ZZZ, which was being conducted for the purpose of instrument proficiency for me, using a view-limiting device while accompanied by a safety pilot. Flight planning indicated that we had sufficient fuel for this mission, and indeed, I have flown this route several times with no issues in other similar aircraft. I was using planned fuel burn of 10 gph, in accordance with performance charts for [this make/model], such as the one we were flying. We checked fuel state prior to the flight both on the gauges, as well as by visual verification on both tanks (both myself and my safety pilot) during the pre-flight inspection. Both tanks were visually noted by both of us as being above the tabs. The flight proceeded uneventfully until the final leg from ZZZ2 to ZZZ. Approximately halfway between the two airports, at an altitude of 6,500 MSL (a little over 3 hours into the flight), the engine developed roughness, then sputtered and quit. We had just changed tanks approximately 2 minutes prior, and I had adjusted the mixture slightly, so I immediately applied full rich mixture, turned the electric fuel pump on, and switched the tanks back. The engine caught almost immediately, and I was able to initiate a full power climbing turn in order to remain near the town of ABC, which I knew had an airport, just in case the engine quit again, since we didn't know the reason for the engine stoppage. After about 2 minutes or less, the engine quit again, and I pitched for best glide, and began searching for the airport, which we initially had difficulty doing, due to the obscuration of the airfield beacon by trees when approaching from the south. We attempted to use the CTAF to turn the runway lights up, and eventually were able to do so, and spotted the runway. Upon identifying my landing site, I then had my safety pilot read the emergency checklist for engine failure, while I performed the action items. We were unable to affect a restart. We then attempted to contact ZZZ Approach (just as this happened, ZZY Approach had handed us off to ZZZ, but before we could establish radio contact, the engine had quit the first time). Unable to reach Approach on the radio, we squawked 7700 on the transponder, then prepared for an emergency landing. We easily had the altitude to make the field, so I utilized S-turns and a forward slip to bleed off altitude for a straight-in approach to RWYXX. We landed safely, (a textbook short field landing) and egressed the aircraft. We could hear sirens as emergency responders from the city of ABC, both fire and police (having been notified by ATC) were en-route to our location. I notified approach via cell phone that we were safe on deck (all personnel on board, as well as the aircraft), and the first responders assisted with towing the aircraft to a parking area. Upon inspecting the aircraft afterwards, we discovered that both tanks were completely empty (both fuel tanks were still reading approximately 1/4 tank on the gauges when the engine first quit, and the left tank gauge continued to show this fuel state even after landing). According to pre-flight planning, we should have had about 1.2 hours of fuel remaining at that point of the flight, which would have allowed us to make it back to ZZZ and have our legal VFR night fuel reserve plus some, so this gauge reading seemed reasonable at the time (although I have never entirely trusted fuel gauges in aircraft, and this incident has greatly deepened that distrust)!My understanding is that the owner will be doing an inspection in the next few days to confirm that there are no fuel leaks or other issues that might have contributed to running out of fuel early. Assuming that no mechanical issues are found at that time, I believe that the following factors are involved:(1) For some reason I thought that fuel at the tabs on this plane was X gallons (Y per side), but I later found that in this aircraft it is Z gallons (A gallons per side out of a Y gallon tank). A contributing factor for this may have been that most of my recent flight time has been in a [different model] for which tabs are indeed Y per side. I may have confused this with the Y gallons per side TOTAL for this aircraft for full tanks, not tabs. (2) It is possible that this aircraft was burning a lot more than 10 gph. I was told afterwards that the aircraft burns more like 15 gph average if you are performing a lot of pattern work (and we had conducted 4 instrument approaches prior to heading home on the final leg). None of the [aircraft] publications that I have substantiate this type of fuel burn for an IO360 engine, but if so, than that would partly explain why we ran out of fuel early. I am not aware of whether this aircraft has any performance modifications that would increase fuel burn. A 15 gph burn rate, even for a short time, would definitely run us out much sooner than expected.Thankfully we were able to safely land engine-out at this small rural airfield, especially given that this happened at night in an airplane that I was relatively unfamiliar with. This incident reinforces the value of proper pre-flight planning and ensuring that accurate information is available in terms of fuel burn as well as fuel tank size, even when operating in the local area on a fairly short flight in terms of distance between points. It also reinforces the value of cruising at higher altitudes when over rugged terrain, especially at night. Lastly, it shows the importance of staying proficient at all aspects of an engine-out emergency. My thanks to all that assisted, from the approach controllers, to the first responders, as well as my safety pilot.
1780871: The following is a list of concerns and questions regarding ZZZ Center's decision to go ATC Zero in the middle of the day as well as the process by which it occurred. I'm going to divide the report into three major issues with details below. I'm not sure how many of my colleagues will file individual reports, but this is a combination of many of our concerns as discussed during and after the event. The three major places we believer safety was jeopardized were: 1) The decision to close in the middle of the day on short notice. 2) Confusion between the published contingency plan and the COVID contingency plan. 3) The decision to not transition into ATC Zero procedures until only 30 minutes prior to the event.1) Why close in the middle of the day?ZZZ Center has had multiple COVID positives since the beginning of the pandemic, and cleaning was always delayed until the mid-shift, when traffic is greatly reduced. In fact, in early Month 1, we had a Controller from the X Area report to work and leave in the middle of the shift because he was feeling sick. He took a test on his way home from work and reported back to the facility that he was indeed COVID positive. His crew finished their shift, the night crew worked their entire shift, and then cleaning occurred on the mid. This is after a confirmed COVID was in the building, working traffic that very day.Yesterday, management became aware of the COVID positive the day before and the person hadn't been in the building since Month 1. However, the decision was made that cleaning had to be done immediately. Why the urgency this time? Closing airspace on a very busy travel day on short notice introduced innumerable safety risks to the system, not to mention greatly impacted the efficiency of the NAS nationwide.2) Confusion regarding contingency plan.ZZZ Center has a published contingency plan, which we review at least annually. Procedures and routes have been developed to allow traffic to continue through the facility should it need to close unexpectedly. Apparently, a separate COVID contingency plan was developed outside of these procedures. There was quite a bit of confusion among the workforce regarding this discrepancy - including a NOTAM being published with the frequency from the existing contingency plan, which was actually not going to be used in this COVID plan.Additional issues from the Controller standpoint included a lack of understanding about what was actually happening to ZZZ Center airspace at XA:X0 local [time] when ATC Zero was declared. The contingency plan seems to indicate that ZZZ Center airspace is to be assumed by ZZZ1 Center and ZZZ2 Center, however ZZZ1 Center was under the assumption that ZZZ Center airspace was to be non-radar. To this end, approximately 25 minutes before ATC zero, an aircraft from ZZZ entered [Sector Y] airspace without a hand off. I called [Sector Z] to call radar on the aircraft, assuming that they were busy changing flight plans and forgot to initiate a hand off. The Controller told me on the line they had 'terminated' the aircraft and they were monitoring ZZZ2 frequency. ZZZ1 Center was in contact with ZZZ2 Center and passing ZZZZZ [Intersection] estimates to the controllers there. I told ZZZ1 we were still open until XA:X0 and Controller told me they were informed we were closed 30 minutes before XA:X0 local.Finally, the COVID route into ZZZ2 ended at ZZZZZ1 at which point we were supposed to issue 'rest of route unchanged.' First of all, most of these aircraft did not have ZZZZZ1 on their route, so rest of route clearance doesn't make sense. Second, any aircraft headed to a northeast airport that got tied back into their route with a direct after ZZZZZ1 went right back into ZZZ Center east area airspace. Once again, the question of who owns that airspace, is it radar on non-radar communications into play. We asked for clarification, which didn't come so we started to issue ZZZZZ1…ZZZ…next fix to go further north and around ZZZ Center.We were never adequately briefed on this new COVID contingency, neither when it was developed, nor on the day it was to be implemented. It seemed every time someone came down from TMU (Traffic Management Unit) or the watch desk, we were being told something different. There was a general feeling among the workforce that this was being made up on the fly.3) Too short of a time frame for implementing contingency plan.When airspace is blocked for special operations, routes are put out hours in advance. There are 'all aircraft must be out of the area by xxxxZ' notes sent to surrounding facilities and published in NOTAMs. These special operations have become fairly routine at ZZZ Center and we still get procedures started early.ATC Zero in the middle of the day is a much more complicated issue affecting a much larger piece of airspace and many more routes. Regardless, the decision was made to operate essentially as normal until the ATC limited at 30 minutes before XA:X0 local. Beginning with the fact that it takes significantly more than 30 minutes to traverse ZZZ airspace, this was not nearly enough time to sterilize the airspace and ensure all remaining aircraft were established on the only acceptable routes through ZZZ when ATC Zero (COVID procedure) has been declared. Below is a small list of the issues this created:- As late as 50 minutes prior to XA:X0, aircraft were still departing ZZZ3 and airborne from airports with 'bad routes.' This created increased workload for sectors ZZ and YY as they tried to get aircraft established on good routing prior to the XA:X0 local ATC Zero.- Sector YY needed a D-side and had (estimated) 15+ tracks as late as 35 minutes prior to XA:X0 local ATC Zero. At a time when we should be well into the transition into ATC Zero procedures, we were still working hard to separate aircraft and resolve conflicts.- Sector YX/ZX took hand offs on two slower moving aircraft near ZZZ4 at approximately 15 minutes prior to filed to ZZZ4 and ZZZ5. There was absolutely no way these aircraft could have been established on the legal contingency routes by XA:X0. We wound up negotiating with ZZZZ1 Center [named] sector to take radar on these aircraft after we issued routes southeast towards their airspace. When we were forced to leave by management at XA:X0 (due to 10 hour shift limitations), these aircraft were switched to ZZZ1 Center, but well into ZZZ Center airspace and not on the established COVID routes. While it is still unclear if ZZZ Center was officially non-radar airspace or not, these aircraft were not on legal non-radar routes. Several controllers were very uncomfortable leaving the airspace in the configuration it was at XA:X0 (myself included). We felt there was more to be done before each of the aircraft we were responsible for was in a safe and legal place.There was a feeling that getting us out before we hit 10 hours was more important than having the procedures fully running properly. Of course, both could have easily occurred if the transition to ATC Zero procedures started earlier.1) Closing in the middle of the day.In the future, short notice ATC Zero procedures should be reserved for immediate, dire emergencies and not be used for cleaning especially days after a positive person was in the building. The decision to go ATC Zero should not be taken lightly and the risks should be carefully measured before the decision is made.2) Confusion regarding contingency plan.A complete, thorough contingency plan needs to be developed and properly briefed to all involved - from OM down to controllers. There should be no confusion about what is going to happen and what each individual facility and sector's responsibilities are to be.3) Too short of a timeframe for ATC Zero implementation.When it is absolutely necessary to go to ATC Zero, the procedures must be implemented earlier. At a minimum, aircraft forecast to be in the affected airspace need to be given routing off of the ground.ATC Zero cannot be declared until each and every single aircraft in the affected airspace is accounted for and on an established contingency route. ZZZ Center went ATC Zero for a mid-day for COVID cleaning. This had not been conducted before during the day shift at ZZZ Center, only on the mid shift. The COVID cleaners were slightly delayed for their cleaning resulting in the airspace being closed longer than Command Center and Management had anticipated. The Operation Manager and all of the Front Line Managers were told that the cleaning was completed in the control room. They all came into the building to see and smell how the environment was inside the control room. Within minutes most of management came back outside dry heaving and coughing severely and said that the areas (Control Room) needed more time for the chemical to settle. After approximately 15 minutes, Management told us to come back into the building. We all initially thought the smell was bad. It was truly hard to breath. After a short amount of time, I was experiencing confusion, headache, sore throat, shortness of breath, nausea and could taste the chemical with my mask on. The taste of the chemical today has still not gone away. It smells and tastes like insecticide. My throat is still a bit sore. Several controllers went home on sick leave because they could not breathe and were coughing. The Operations Manager and all of the Front Line Managers left the control room multiple times because the fumes were so bad. They needed fresh air.There was not enough time between when the COVID cleaning taking place and when we were told to come back into the building. I want to know what chemical I was breathing in for over 5 hours. I believe this harmed me. Tech Operations stated that everything was saturated in the control room. What we were breathing in was not safe.
1780881: Aircraft X was on the ZZZZZ departure climbing out of ZZZ. The [Sector X] Controller climbed the aircraft to FL330 and flashed the aircraft to [Sector Y] who followed the AIT and flashed it on to me working [Sector XY]. I recognized a limited aircraft at FL360 so I waited until there were no longer a factor and I looked over and did not see a [Sector Z] Controller at the other end of the room. I called [Sector X D side] and APPREQed control for climb for Aircraft X. The Controller said approved as requested. I climbed the aircraft to FL390 and violated Sector Z without a point out.I made several mistakes in this situation. I had known that [sector] Z was open since I had shipped multiple aircraft to that sector but when I looked over at the sector I did not see a Controller at [Sector Z]. The view of the [Sector Z Controller was blocked by the Sector X Controller. I did not see the Controller sitting behind the Sector X Controller.Another big contributing factor in this situation is that since Month during the COVID pandemic and the reduced traffic, we almost never opened sector Z. Now that traffic has been picking up and we have been utilizing the sector more often I have made this mistake. During the COVID posture we typically gave sector A control to climb on the ZZZ departures. That could also create a problem once sector XY opens.I needed to pay more attention to the current sector configurations.
1780882: Aircraft X departed JNU for ZZZ, but changed destination shortly after to return to JNU because the pilot reported that ZZZ winds would not allow for an approach. Aircraft X initially climbed to 090, but requested descent to 080 for moderate icing. I cleared Aircraft X back to the JNU airport via direct SSR direct, to expect the LDA Z 8 approach, as requested.I cleared Aircraft X for the LDA Z 8 approach, to cross SSR at or above 060. Shortly after progressing SSR, the aircraft transmitted that they were back in the icing and had 'quite a bit of ice on the wing' and said they were unsure if they would be able to maintain the transition altitude of 056 until LYNNS intersection. The aircraft then descended to 052, below the approach altitude. I issued a low altitude alert, and instructed Aircraft X to climb to meet the transition altitude. Aircraft X reported they would attempt to climb, but were unable and appeared to level off at 050 in a 060 MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude), and requested to transition over to the RNAV W 8 approach via JIGMI, as the approach had a lower transition altitude. Seeing as the aircraft had already progress JIGMI, I asked if they would be able to establish themselves on to a published portion of the approach if I provided a heading to join. the pilot said affirmative, so I issued a 10 degree turn to the right to join the RNAV W 8 approach, and to steer the aircraft away form higher terrain to the NW, as it was clear they would be unable to climb. I then informed the pilot that I was providing priority handling for them. Aircraft X was able to maintain 050 until joining the RNAV W 8 approach, at which time I issued the approach clearance and confirmed that the aircraft would be able to maintain the new transition altitudes of that approach. The pilot confirmed that they would, and was able to safely fly the approach to landing.
1780908: Three flights, three last minute gate changes, full on full off on through flight, weather delays, etc. Busy with pre-COVID like Ops tempo. We got a last minute gate change and when we got to our new aircraft we called for push, same callsign, from our old gate. Surprised Ground, but no conflicts noted.Ground Ops is struggling to keep up with changes and weather issues using COVID Manning and Procedures. Constant gate changes, especially on through flights, doesn't seem to be the best solution. Pilots need to be aware of post COVID procedures irregularities and adapt accordingly. This was a simple mistake but indicative of a larger issue.Called for push from wrong gate.
1780917: We were on a visual approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ at 3,000 feet. Approach cleared us for a visual approach about 7 miles out and we were giving a heading towards the FAF following an airbus. PF set 2,000 feet in the MCP and we began a slow descent heading inbound to the airport. ATC issued a 'low altitude alert' at about 2,300 feet. We leveled off and intercepted the G/S just past the FAF. In addition, we had to rapidly slow since the airbus in front slowed rapidly and ATC wanted us to slow to approximately 150 knots or less. They really did not leave us much lateral room. We slowed and configured while descending. We were never near an obstacle, nor were we a threat to another aircraft. We were still above the 1,000 feet stable approach criteria (1,300 to 1,500 feet) and met the criteria proof to reaching 1,000 feet. We were lower than what was normally flow for that area but still seamed safe. Again on a visual approach. PF stated that he read 2,000 feet at the FAF and misread the altitude. The FAF altitude is 2,800 feet. I did not reverify it since we were visual and I was working on setting up radios and configuration for landing. I assumed he saw it correctly.I can't find where we violated anything. We were a little low for the area but still in a safe position to land and had visual clearance from all obstacles. I know next time to verify the altitude in the MCP from the chart myself. That is that only thing that may have stopped the lower alt in the first place. On receiving landing clearance, I set 2,000 feet in the altitude window and planned to descend to that altitude at ZZZZZ, the FAF. I misread the approach plate. The correct altitude at ZZZZZ is 2,800 feet. The Tower gave us a Low Altitude Alert at 2,200 MSL in VMC and we maintained that altitude (we were nearly at glideslope intercept) until glideslope intercept. We landed uneventfully.
1780931: During pushback, the tug driver did not use proper terminology. I understand that the contract ramp personnel work many different airlines, but they should have a working knowledge on the aircraft that they are pushing back, as well as some type of standard phraseology and verbiage.Upon completion of the pushback, the tug driver asked me to set the parking brake, which I did, and using proper terminology, I told him 'Brakes Set, Pressure Normal.' A few minutes later, he said to me, 'Have a good flight.' I asked him if the tow bar was disconnected and if the bypass pin had been removed, and he said 'Not yet, I'll tell you when they are.' A few minutes later, he said again, 'Have a good flight' and he disconnected the headset before I could ask him again if the tow bar had been disconnected and if the bypass pin had been removed. I rang the Ground Call button, and I was trying to use hand signals to have the wing walker inform the tug driver that I needed to talk to him on the headset. During this time, I did see the tug backing away from the aircraft, with the tow bar, and a ramp person walking away with the bypass pin in her hand. It appeared that the ramp personnel were finally starting to understand that I was trying to get someone back on the headset, when I gave them a thumbs up signal. The ramp person gave me the thumbs up signal, and they knew we were all set to go. I received the proper Salute, started engines and we taxied away.The tug driver never told me that the tow bar had been disconnected and that the bypass pin had been removed. The tug driver needs to have a working knowledge of the proper terminology to inform the Captain that the towbar has been disconnected and that the bypass pin has been removed, and to wait for the Captain to tell him that it is OK to disconnect the headset, not to just disconnect the headset on his own.Communication is paramount to prevent an accident, and in my opinion, this tug driver did not understand nor use proper verbiage/procedure during the pushback.
1780932: During cruise flight, the Purser called to advise that the passenger seated in X was not complying with established face mask policy. Per the flight attendants, the passenger was tearing layers of the mask away. The flight attendants offered a new face mask from onboard PPE provisions but the customer refused. The Purser advised multiple de-escalation attempts were made along with the flight deck making a PA. The Purser advised that non-compliance continued and, ultimately, the operations center was advised. A customer service representative was requested to meet the flight after coordination with the Inflight crew and operations center security. Purser advised that a FA a report would be submitted for this event.
1780934: We were in cruise flight in smooth air with the autopilot on and flying our cost index profile. The Captain was on his rest break. I was the non flying pilot in the left seat, and the Flying First Officer was in the right seat. We were at 37,000 ft. and M.83 in smooth air when the airspeed started climbing as we encountered a mountain wave. The flying First Officer immediately began to reduce the throttles and came all the way to idle as the airspeed kept increasing. At this point, I asked if he would like me to deploy the speedbrakes to assist in the effort to keep the aircraft from over speeding. I began deploying the speedbrakes, but the aircraft accelerated slightly above maximum operating to M.875. We maintained idle thrust and speed brakes until clear of the mountain wave.We then submitted a PIREP electronically and also notified ATC who said we were the first report. However, shortly thereafter another aircraft also reported mountain wave activity. Total airspeed fluctuation was plus or minus about 15 to 20 kts.
1780938: On the transition to an ILS Approach. Once we were handed over to Approach we were given different speeds along the approach which is typical. It was IMC with a reported ceiling of 700 ft. We were given 160 kts. and handed over to Tower frequency. The aircraft we were following at the time was 5 miles ahead of us. Approximately 3 miles outside of the final approach fix I saw on the TCAS an aircraft turning a right base and appeared to be sequencing in front of us. Tower shortly after instructed us to slow to approach speed which was 135 kts. We were then told we were following Aircraft Y. The Aircraft Y was approximately 2 miles ahead of us. I told the First Officer to plan on a go-around. I had fully briefed the approach prior to Top of Descent. Tower then asked the Aircraft Y to do a midfield landing due to separation. Around 1,400 ft. we were told to go-around. It was a normal go-around profile and we were vectored back for a normal landing. Crew was on approach. Initial ATIS reported ceilings 400 feet and 1/2 mile visibility. Crew elected to transfer controls to the Captain and execute an auto-land approach for currency and to increase safety margin. Approach was commencing normally with positive airspeed control by ATC. Approximately 4 miles from Final Approach Fix ATC vectored an aircraft onto final ahead of us. Aircraft rolled out approximately 2 miles ahead on final as indicated by TCAS. We were handed off to Tower and given clearance to land number two. Preceding aircraft was instructed to expedite turnoff after landing due to close interval. At approximately 800 feet. and at the top of the IMC layer, Tower canceled landing clearance and directed a climb to 2,000 feet and track localizer inbound. Crew conducted a normal go-around. Aircraft was vectored to a second approach and a normal landing ensued.
1780939: Cleared for ILS XXR approach into ZZZ outside of ZZZZZ maintain 3,000 until established. VMC but too hazy to see runway at 12 miles final. Autopilot was engaged and LOC was armed but the aircraft did not intercept and we flew thru LOC course. I turned off autopilot and autothrottles to attempt re-intercept of localizer however flight directors were giving far right correction with LOC indices correcting slightly left. We were far right of course, so FD guidance was completely inaccurate and LOC indices should have been making far correction to left which they were not. We attempted to determine source of the problem but were unsuccessful doing so. We cycled the ILS radio panel, but no help. We asked for Go-around and were given instructions by ATC. On second approach attempt LOC and GS captured and an uneventful landing was made.
1780940: Flight operated normally. After landing in ZZZZ and beginning flight planning for next leg I realized I had not signed the release prior to departure for the previous flight. I had just returned to the line after not flying for almost 7 months due to the pandemic. We were on a delay due to flight attendant staffing. I reviewed the release, saved it to my iPad, briefed my crew and even spoke with the Dispatcher prior to departure about the Flight Attendant issue and our timeline for departure. However I missed signing the release. Contributing factors include, lack of recent experience due to the pandemic, inability to print the dispatch release displayed on the ACARS.
1780942: During Exterior Preflight inspection it was noted that the Number 2 engine was actively leaking fuel. Maintenance was consulted and it was determined continued operation was possible providing a successful engine run was completed and the fuel leak had stopped. Maintenance Control was contacted and approval for an engine run was approved. I briefed the ramp and maintenance personnel on the logistics of the gate engine run. The engine run was completed at the gate. Shortly afterwards we received verification from the Maintenance Technician that we were good as the leak had stopped. We were informed that the maintenance release would be processed shortly. Two minutes later we noted on the iPad that the deferral mentioned by the Technician was processed. As the Number 2 engine was running at the gate and I briefed that we would push as soon as Maintenance said we were good we released the brake and commenced the push. In-flight we received a message to contact the Dispatch. After landing a Manager mentioned we may have departed without a maintenance release. We retained the same plane for the subsequent flight with a valid maintenance release with no maintenance action. Pre-flight planning completed and aircraft had valid maintenance release. Fuel leak found on Number 2 engine during walk around. Local maintenance consulted. Technician told us engine can be started and run at the gate and if fuel leak stopped, issue would be put on deferral, and we could just push out and continue. Received authorization from Maintenance Control for engine run and all personnel were briefed on procedure. Number 2 engine was started and run at the gate with Technician on the headset. Technician told us that fuel leak stopped after startup so paperwork would be completed immediately, deferral issued and we were good to go. Flight pushed back very soon after as briefed, taxied out and took off. Message was received in flight to contact Dispatch management upon landing ZZZ1. Called and [was] told apparently flight departed without valid maintenance release. We received a valid maintenance release and flew same aircraft to ZZZ2 without incident.
1780946: Operated Flight ABC ZZZ to ZZZ1 and approximately 75 nm east of ZZZZZ [fix] I checked the EICAS status page and noticed ADD for the APU oil. A couple of minutes later we got a status message stating APU oil was low. I SATCOMed Dispatch and conferenced Maintenance Control. Decision was made to divert to ZZZ. No emergency declared - normal arrival. When maintenance techs were in the cockpit after arrival they stated that the APU oil was checked via EICAS as part of the ETOPS pre-departure service check. While speaking with the tech they stated that the technician working in the tail just added three quarts of oil which they said is just 'a lot' for the APU doesn't hold much more. APU started for a leak check and it auto shutdown twice. It was said that there were no leaks. The tech stated they found it strange when looking at history that no oil had been added in two months. It was theorized by maintenance that the quantity unit may have been stuck showing full when it wasn't. Flight was re-dispatched with a different aircraft. I subsequently found out that the oil quantity unit and oil pressure switch were replaced to fix this problem.
1780947: While approximately 2 hours from our destination, we discovered that ZZZZ1 weather would not allow us to land at destination. We made a decision with fuel and time to hold and then subsequently divert to ZZZZ2. The communication barrier was difficult with the controllers and while that took place we were also using the radio for Dispatch. I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and was coordinating the divert with Dispatch and the handling in ZZZZ2. Task saturation after a long flight was certainly a challenge. I also was having freezing issues with Jepp FD pro. After being handed to ATC, we had the approach and plan in place for the approach Runway XX. On the decent the controllers left us very high even after multiple requests for lower. The PF (Pilot Flying) was using FLCH and max speed brakes most of the time. We were able to get to an appropriate altitude safely. I had a brief moment of thought about still being in FLCH on decent and through saturation, I failed to mention it. Inside the IAF I set the TDZE as normal and confirmed with crew, as we were cleared the approach. We had still been descending constantly from events before, we never really stopped descending since just after the divert was made. As we were in the arc, we were completely configured for landing and I noticed that we had descended below the published altitude on the ARC. I quickly realized we had been still in FLCH and immediately said to stop decent. We were approximately 400-500 ft. Low. And after arresting settled at about 600 below. The PF and crew were in VMC conditions. CAVOK. We were approximately 1/2 to 3/4 of the way through the arc once I noticed. We had the airport in sight and the PF elected to stay at the approximate pattern altitude as we were over water in VMC and had the airport in sight and about to turn final. The approach continued visually and the PF made a normal landing and taxi to hard stand.
1780949: I awoke at XA:00 on Date and was called just a few hours later and told I was being placed back on rest, and given a XP:00 assignment. I don't understand how I'm supposed to be able to function, with less than 12 hours to adjust. I attempted to go to sleep at XJ:00 but laid awake till almost XM:00. I was awakened just after XM:00 when my phone received a text alert that my schedule had changed. I have no way to silence text alerts without also silencing all phone calls. I attempted to go back to sleep but was stressed that I would sleep through the call and could never fall back to sleep. Scheduling finally called me at XR:00, giving me absolute minimum notice to show, when I was forced to call in fatigued. I understand that this type of assignment is currently legal on paper, it shouldn't be, but I have to tell you that I flew transatlantic flights for 8 years and was never as fatigued as I have been on Reserve under this domestic FAR 117 rules. This is ridiculous. This is the second time in only 10 days that I was switched from day to night duty with less than 12 hours notice and after being awake for less than 5-6 hours. I want to make our system work so that the flights can be covered, but this current system is a system of 'gamesmanship'. No one is on the same team. Why don't we have a system where everyone wants the system to work to get the planes and passengers where they need to be? It just seems like it has become a war between the company and the union and not a great place to work anymore.
1780950: While conducting preparations for arrival into MEX, crew discovered the following charting error: All ILS and RNP (RNAV) approach charts to Runway 05R depict the final course to as 055 degrees. However the 11-0 MAVEK Transition to ILS DME2 Runway 05R dated Date depicts the ILS Runway 05R localizer course as 053 degrees (a discrepancy of 2 degrees).Of note: Course 053 degrees corresponds to the depicted final course to the VOR DME Runway 05L/R (13-1).
1780952: Upon taxi out, Ground Control issued us a clearance to taxi via 'B' and 'D' to Runway 4L. At that time there were multiple aircraft taxiing in the ramp area. Shortly thereafter, Ground then issued a clearance to a 767 on 'B' holding short of 'K' to 'give way to the Guppy, and taxi to 4L.' EWR Ground control's nonstandard phraseology of referring to a 737 colloquially as a 'guppy' has the potential to cause confusion and an increased potential for a deviation or incident due to misunderstanding.
1780959: First leg arrives ZZZZ mid evening, and crew arrives hotel at approximately close to midnight, after a 13-hour duty all-nighter, rests until van departure the next evening ZZZZ time , for a report time 2 hours later and a 2-leg 14:20 duty day with 10+ hours of flying to ZZZZ1 and back followed by another 1.5-2 hours to get back to the ZZZZ hotel. With a 3-person crew, and the FAR117 limitations, the ZZZZ1 turn begins with no one properly rested (due to the 3-person crew, each crewmember gets at most 3 hours of rest on the red-eye to ZZZZ on the first night, and arrives at hotel just after Window of Circadian Low (WOCL), unable to get much restorative rest. The next night's report time is at the *beginning* of the WOCL, meaning two nights in a row of disrupted sleep (unrelated to the ZZZZ1 turn, but indicative of the poorly-built nature of this trip, the third duty period of the 5-day pairing also includes a redeye, for a total of 3 min-rest 3-pilot redeyes in 5 days). Concerning the ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZZ legs, because of the 117 restrictions, depending how the Relief Pilot (RP) and PM split the first leg or part of the 2nd, and the expected flight time of the ZZZZ-ZZZZ1 leg, no one gets decent rest. In our pairing, I as the RP slept first on the outbound leg for 2 hours, and the PM slept next for 3, and the PF slept the entire return leg (2.5 hrs). This was FAR117 compliant, but due to pairing construction is essentially too little, at the wrong time, and contributed to a degradation in safety. It is not helped by a 2-hour ground sit (during which it's impossible to rest because the countries authorities enter the airplane for a security sweep and postflight / preflight duties must be accomplished, and the constant loud noises and aircraft motion from cargo loading/unloading). So the RP and PM sleep a very small amount during the WOCL, and the PF doesn't get a rest opportunity until after the WOCL, when it may no longer be possible to sleep.This is bananas. ZZZZ1, and the country's airspace in general, is among our more challenging operations (language, altimetry, nonstandard ATC phraseology and procedures, night/weather, unfamiliarity with fix names, etc.). Setting up a minimum crew with back-to-back red eyes and little rest opportunity in that environment is dangerous. And the crew is then left to consider a fatigue call on the ground in ZZZZ1 - one of the worst places in the world to stop the operation for crew and airline alike.
1780986: We experienced a sudden engine failure on engine 2 while cruising at FL330. While in cruise the planes speed slowly crept up towards red line so the Captain pulled back the power to prevent any type of over speed of the aircraft. He had the power at idle for about 1 or 2 seconds then began to smoothly bring the power up. Either as he brought it up or within a few seconds we felt the engine fail and got an engine 2 FAIL EICAS caution. The Captain continued flying and took the radios as well as he told me to run the QRH. We ran the engine fail QRH and the NAP checklists that the QRH led us to. During this time we attempted an APU assisted restart because we the number 2 engine still had oil, hydraulic fluid, was not frozen and to the best of our knowledge had not taken significant damage. On the attempted restart there was no movement on N1 or N2 at all. At that time we deemed an engine restart was not possible. We also decided on diverting to ZZZ2 while doing this, because we were just passing it, it has a nearly 10,000 feet runway, and we had two alternates because of what we assumed was the possibility of fog later in the night so we didn't want to continue north. We finished all QRH, checklists, and talked to the flight attendants and passengers and made an uneventful landing. After stopping on the runway the trucks checked for damage then followed us as we taxied to the gate under our own power. Loss of number 2 engine during cruise.Followed QRH, advised ATC, diverted.
1781021: The fatigue call that was made by myself and my First Officer was predicated by a very long day the day before as well as schedule changes on the day of the fatigue call. On [date 1], we flew 9.1 hours from ZZZ to ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 to ZZZ3. We had 30 minute or less turns the whole day, both passenger legs required lav services, and refueling was required at each stop. On approach into ZZZ1 we also had to break off the approach as the aircraft in front of us slowed down more than ATC anticipated. On approach into ZZZ2 we picked up ice and frost underneath the wing clinging to the bottom of the cold soaked fuel tanks. We attempted to start the process for de-icing, but multiple aircraft had to be moved on the ramp for that to occur per the FBO. By the time the passengers arrived and bags were loaded the majority had melted and I used my hands to remove the rest. The flight down to ZZZ3 was 4.0 hours due to headwinds and we arrived at night time. The next day was only supposed to be one leg from ZZZ3 to ZZZ4 then it grew to include ZZZ4 to ZZZ5 once we got to the hotel. Only about 30 minutes prior to departure from ZZZ3 the next day were we informed that the day had grown to ZZZ3 to ZZZ4 to ZZZ6 to ZZZ7 and then once we arrived in ZZZ4 it had grown again to include a 4th leg back to ZZZ5 from ZZZ7. On our way into ZZZ7 we were informed by ATC that ZZZ Center would be going ATC zero for COVID cleaning and once we landed no clearances could be issued northbound. This would necessitate staying in ZZZ7 for the night and a show at XM:0X am to arrive at ZZZ5 for the passenger leg at XP:00 am. The fatigue from [Date 1] and [Date 2] would have only been amplified by the early show and so we decided it was not safe to continue as scheduled once we arrived in ZZZ7 for the night. The fatigue was further evidenced by the fact that while we were getting our bags out at ZZZ7 we discovered that a passenger [bag] from the ZZZ3 to ZZZ4 leg had been missed and was still in the aircraft.
1781036: In cruise I messaged Dispatch and asked the RVR for [Runway] XXR. They told me 1400 for [Runway] XXR. About 30 minutes from arrival we started our brief. We briefed the arrival and the approach plate for [Runway]. We then briefed the CAT2 checklist. We both put 705 feet in our DH and verified it. We did the decent check and verified it again. Did the approach check and was getting vectors to [Runway] XXR. Gear down flaps 45 before the marker. I called 1,000 feet cleared to land when I knew something was wrong. I couldn't grasp why we only had 300 feet left to go missed. Told the First Officer something wasn't right. We hit minimums at 705 feet AGL and I called the missed. Did the missed approach, cleaned up aircraft and did the checklist. Didn't take me long to figure out what I did. The RA for [Runway] XXR is 116 feet. We put the new DH in and took our time to get set up for approach. We got vectors on the LOC and shot the approach to a landing.We both missed the right number for the DH. I knew the approach would be to minimums so I was looking at chart in cruise so I wouldn't miss anything. Ended up on a go around at 700 feet AGL because we had the MDA in. It was first flight of day we both felt good. Just the low visibility at destination caused a threat.Even after the lengthy briefing and checklist usage the DH was still put in there wrong. What I have learned over my career is not to get upset at the moment you realize you did something wrong. Great training over the years and good CRM has trained me to fly the airplane. Run the appropriate checklists and then discuss what happened at a safe time later. We incorrectly set the 705 feet in the DH for a CAT 2 approach and logically got the mins aural alert more than 500 feet early. We executed a go-around, set up the DH properly and flew the second approach normally.
1781064: A little while after reaching cruise altitude, the flight attendants contacted us to let us know that there was a passenger who was not complying with the mask policy. They were handling it per their guidance and keeping us informed. Later in the flight there had been some other problems that they had informed us about. The First Officer and I had completed a bathroom rotation just before starting down into ZZZ when we got a call from the flight attendants informing us they were [having problems with this passenger]. They just wanted to be sure we knew this. I asked them to let us know if there were any problems. Several minutes later, we received a call that this passenger had not taken kindly to the warning and had become 'verbally combative.' I thanked them for letting us know, and asked if everyone was okay. They replied yes, they were. I asked them to keep us informed if there were any changes of if anything escalated, they said they would. At this point we had begun the descent on the arrival into ZZZ, the First Officer had been flying the whole leg. He had been managing the radios as well while I was talking to the flight attendants. I considered that while the situation currently was Level 1, I felt it was most prudent to get the aircraft on the ground to protect my crew and the other passengers. Additionally, felt it would reduce my workload as well as my First Officer's if we requested priority handling. I told the First Officer what I was considering and why, and asked if he had any considerations. He agreed that was a good choice. I then requested priority handling with ZZZ approach and informed them of SOB and fuel remaining. I had sent an ACARS message to Dispatch informing them of our situation. I called ZZZ ops and informed them of the same. I then checked in with the flight attendants to ensure things were okay, which they were. I informed them we were accepting priority handling and would be on the ground as soon as possible. As we passed through 10,000 feet we kept the speed up around 315 knots to expedite our arrival. We were given radar vectors to a visual Runway X and landed uneventfully. We had to wait a few minutes for our gate as it was occupied. We pulled into the gate. The passenger disembarked and the situation was over. There were no injuries. After the plane was empty the crew got together in the front of the airplane for a debrief of the situation. At the end of the debrief I asked the flight attendants if they were okay and would be comfortable with continuing. They all felt that they were okay to continue. When the First Officer and I debriefed, I asked him the same and he was good. I took a moment to assess myself and determined I was good to continue as well.It is worth noting that the flight attendants did a very good job of keeping us informed as to the status of the situation. This was helpful and good crew CRM. They were clear in their communication, calm and professional. My First Officer also was a model of CRM and performed exceptionally to include his aircraft handling to expedite our arrival. Passenger wasn't complying with mask usage after being repeatedly requested to by flight attendants. Flight attendants issued warning after which passenger became verbally aggressive.
1781083: On approach to ZZZ, Initially the weather report was 3/4 SM visibility, so I informed the controller that I needed 1SM to shoot the approach due to my high minimums status. The Controller gave me direct ZZZ VOR and Hold northeast as published at 6,000 feet. I began heading direct to the VOR, when the controller came back and gave me the updated visibility at 1SM. So I accepted vectors to the approach. As I neared the FAF, I knew that I would need to be able to see the approach lights and runway in a low visibility situation, so I attempted to move the sun visor back to its stowed position. The visor became stuck, which is normal for these airplanes so I pushed harder. As I did that, the visor suddenly released itself and hit me in the face, causing a dull pain and immediate swelling. I touched the area and came back with a lot of blood on my hand, so I concentrated on flying the approach using standard procedures and call-outs and getting back on the ground. Unfortunately, I reached mins and did not see the runway environment, so I called out 'minimums, missed approach' and began the missed approach procedure according to standard procedures and call-outs. The controller attempted to give me a hold over the ZZZ VOR, but as I was bleeding and didn't know how long I would need to hold I chose to divert back to ZZZ1. I confirmed this decision after reaching cruise and having center call company Dispatch. Center informed me that I was a [priority] aircraft and would be treated as such as I had initially requested paramedics upon arrival. Upon reaching cruise however, I used my phone (which was off) as a mirror and concluded that I did not need medical assistance. So I informed Center of this change. I completed the flight back to ZZZ1 with no further issues. Paramedics met me at the ramp anyway, along with Airport OPS. They did not request my information and sent me on my way after cleaning the blood off of my face and neck. I then called dispatch and the Chief Pilots office to inform them of the situation.When the sun visor hit me in the face and I found blood on my hand. The sun visor in this airplane is in poor condition and gets stuck on the rail constantly. This in addition to the fact that I was very task saturated and didn't realize that the bleeding wasn't as bad as I had initially thought. I made the division to divert as I was performing a missed approach and wasn't aware of how severe the injury was. I knew the other airports in the vicinity were not suitable so I decided to go back to ZZZ1 as I knew it was 800-1000 foot OVC and I would have no issues. If I had moved the sun visor earlier that would have been beneficial, aside from that it could definitely use some TLC.
1781084: Departing ZZZ Runway XX at XA23, Aircraft X encountered a complete hydraulic failure on initial climbout. Conditions at the time were winds out of the north west 14 knots Gusting 23 knots. The annunciator panel indicated that both the Left and Right Hydraulics Failure annunciation and a cross check of the hydraulic pressure gauge confirmed this with an indication of low pressure. An After Takeoff Checklist was completed followed by the Hydraulic System Failure Checklist, Landing Gear Emergency Extension Checklist and a verification of Gear 3 down and green. The decision was made to continue to the destination of ZZZ1 airport due to the better runway environment, ILS, emergency services and the nature of the windy conditions in ZZZ. ATC was advised and a request for vectors to the IAF for the ILS XY at ZZZ1 airport was made. ZZZ1 airport conditions were reporting winds out of the South West at 4 knots, 10 miles and clear skies. Upon landing and rollout a loud vibration was noticed which appeared to be from the nose-wheel area and possible cantering nose wheel or a tire issue. Ground crew was requested to inspect the condition of the landing gear and wheel well area before continuing the taxi and any possible damage that may have incurred by the aircraft or to the runway and taxiway environment. After an all clear from Ground Ops, a normal taxi without nose-wheel hydraulic steering took place proceeded with engine shutdown at the FBO. Upon initial inspection, hydraulic fluid was visually confirmed leaking from the wheel well of Engine #1. All cargo was unloaded from the aircraft and Dispatch and Department of Maintenance coordinated a ferry flight after an inspection by the mechanic. The ferry flight was canceled shortly after taxi upon the realization that the nose-wheel vibration and shimmy was too excessive to be able to execute a normal takeoff and the aircraft was grounded for further mechanical inspection.
1781085: Controller had to have had a mask on as his communications were muffled and thus hard to understand. We read back clearance to FL230 and as we were passing through 22,500 he said we were only cleared to FL220. He said to just continue to FL230 and that is what we did. No conflict was noted.
1781086: I was the AFA (A Flight Attendant). Every part of the flight (boarding, climb, cruise, etc.) seemed to be going fine and seemed standard. When the pilots told us to prepare the cabin for arrival, I decided to look over the PAX (Passenger) manifest before tossing it. I had used it during the flight but only looked at part of it. To be honest, I didn't read over it before we departed. When I read over it toward the end of the flight, I noticed that one PAX was listed as a Special Assistance Passenger. This PAX was listed as needing a wheelchair and as blind. At no point was I aware that we had a PAX with a visual impairment. The PAX was boarded first and the person who pushed his wheelchair stowed the PAX's luggage. When interacting with the PAX on boarding, I handed him a sanitizing wipe and he seemed to have no trouble getting the wipe from me or getting to his seat, although I didn't really watch him go to his seat. At no point did the gate agent inform us that we had a PAX with a visual impairment nor did the person who pushed the wheelchair. When the B Flight Attendant asked the gate agent if we had any specials (for the PAX count form) the gate agent said we had one wheelchair. There was no mention of a PAX with a visual impairment.We did the standard briefings (announcements and safety demo), but neither of us provided a one-on-one briefing with the PAX. We were unaware of his visual impairment. After I realized our mistake on descent, I wasn't sure what to do. I had a brief conversation with the PAX, and he seemed to look me in the eye for the conversation. After I played the final descent announcement, I showed the B Flight Attendant the manifest and how it showed a PAX listed as blind. She was surprised to see it. We discussed our situation in regard to the PAX and the possibility of writing a report.After we landed, the PAX gathered his belongings and deplaned without help. He also told the person waiting with the wheelchair that he didn't need it. He was traveling alone and without the assistance of a service animal. He only used a simple walking cane, not a red and white cane frequently used by people with visual impairments. He gave me no reason to think that he was visually impaired, but I understand that some disabilities are not apparent. When all the PAX had deplaned, I informed the Captain of what had happened and asked for advice. He said to fill out an report because we didn't do a required briefing. The B Flight Attendant and I knew that one-on-one briefings are required, we didn't know the PAX was visually impaired.I am concerned and upset that we potentially caused a safety incident with a PAX with a visual impairment. This is unacceptable. I hope to use this as a learning experience and pay closer attention to the PAX manifest before shutting the boarding door and proactively asking all gate agents about special assist PAX that we may have onboard. I say this with caution, though. We don't always receive the correct manifest, we sometimes receive incomplete manifests with no PAX information, and sometimes we don't even receive a manifest at all. While in the end, it was my responsibility to confirm with the gate agent about special assist PAX, I feel like there was a breakdown of communication between the gate agent and me. I wonder if the gate agent knew there was a visually impaired PAX on the flight. Perhaps there could be strengthened training for gate agents and flight attendants for recognizing special assist PAX. For flight attendants, also what to do if a special assist PAX is discovered during flight and certain briefings did not occur, as in our case. As stated before, I didn't know what to do in regard to the PAX.I understand the severe safety hazards not providing a one-on-one briefing could have caused if something went wrong during flight. I hope to use this as a lesson learned and not solely rely on being informed of all special assist PAX by a gate agent. In other words, I need to be more proactive, and I need to use my resources more wisely. My hope is that this can be used as a lesson for all flight attendants so that incidents like this don't happen again. We are first and foremost a safety industry, and we failed to keep to our safety standards.
1781087: While executing the ILS to [Runway] XXR at ZZZ, ATC informed us that we were following a heavy and instructed us to slow to 170kts. The Captain and I saw the other aircraft on TCAS and judged the distance to be six or seven miles. We discussed the possibility of wake turbulence but we didn't think the spacing was an issue. Then, after switching the tower, at around 3,000 feet, we were instructed to start slowing to our final approach speed. We then configured the aircraft for landing and started running the landing checklist. While listening and responding to the Captain's checklist callouts, I thought I heard someone say 'approach clearance canceled, maintain 3,000', but I was unsure of the call sign. This was partly because the Captain and I were in the middle of running a checklist and partly because there was another aircraft on frequency that had a very similar call sign. We were Company X Callsign ABBC and the aircraft ahead of the heavy was Company X Callsign ADDC (there were at least three instances during the arrival where an instruction was given and we weren't 100% sure who it was for). I interrupted the Captain and told him that I thought tower had just canceled someone's approach clearance and asked him to query ATC to see if it was for us. The controller responded with a very urgent tone and said 'That is affirm, Callsign ABBC your approach clearance is canceled, maintain present heading and climb to 3,000. I'll have a turn for you in just a second.' As the captain was responding to ATC, I pressed the heading button to maintain our present heading as instructed, but I was confused as to what to do next. At this point we were around 2,400 feet (about 2,000 feet AFE), so a hard go-around using the TO/GA button was not required. I was not really mentally prepared for the go-around and was having trouble deciding what to do next, but ATC sounded like they wanted me to start climbing immediately to 3,000 feet, which was already set in the altitude window, so I reacted to his instruction by hitting FLCH. This caused the aircraft to apply full throttle and pitch up to maintain our current approach speed of about 145kts. We maintain this climb for several seconds until I was able to dial the speed up and get the aircraft accelerating. With everything happening so fast, and not really being mentally prepared for a go-around, I called gear up while the flaps were still at 5 which caused the landing gear warning to sound. It was a very sloppy go-around but I don't think the aircraft was ever in an unsafe state.This was my first go-around in the actual aircraft. However, I have mentally rehearsed and practiced enough hard go-arounds in sim training that the procedure is pretty much automatic and I can execute it without much thinking required. However, I can only recall doing a soft go-around once during FTD training and, as I recall, in that scenario we were not yet configured for landing and the altitude assigned was below us, so it was a simple matter of stopping the descent and flying the assigned heading. We also discussed soft go-arounds vs hard go-arounds in training and I had recalled that using TO/GA was optional but not really preferred during a soft-go around. I think there needs to be more training on soft go-arounds and the SOP should give more guidance as to preferred methods in various scenarios. Currently, the SOP does not give much guidance on the subject other than reminding the pilot to retract flaps at the F-bug or XX knots above green dot. After landing, the Captain and I discussed what I could have done better. He suggested, and I agreed, that the best course of action would have been to press ALT to stop the descent and then start accelerating before starting our climb. However, after replaying it in my head all night, I came to the conclusion that, given the fact that ATC wanted me to climb, it would have been perfectly acceptable to switch to heading mode and then press TO/GA and execute my normalgo-around actions and callouts, even though we were well above 1,000 feet AFE. This would ensure the aircraft was maintaining a safe speed while we began to reconfigure the aircraft and would have eliminated a lot of confusion that I created while I pondered what technique I should use to get us to 3,000 feet while also cleaning up the aircraft. Perhaps this should be the preferred method to execute a soft-go around when fully configured for landing and a climb is required. But perhaps there's another aspect of it that I'm not considering. The technique of pressing ALT and accelerating aircraft prior to starting the climb also seems like it would work in most situations. That's why I think the SOP should give more guidance on the subject. If there were a preferred method spelled out in the SOP, then it would eliminate a lot of the confusion and both pilots would be on the same page instead of debating on a technique for a procedure that is rarely used when there isn't really time to stop and think about it.This experience has also taught me to be prepared for a go-around at all times, not just when below 1,000 feet on an approach. Although, the spacing behind the heavy looked good to us, we should have been more prepared for the possibility that ATC would call for a go-around unexpectedly.
1781094: On left downwind for Runway 35L OKC at 3,000 feet, co-pilot reported seeing a quad-copter drone approximately 15 feet from the left wing tip.
1781102: Ever since we began wearing masks I am fearful of my job. I am getting headaches and at times migraines. When I get a headache, I am cranky so not always nice to passengers. I cannot communicate properly with my [coworkers], my customers, the agents, etc. In an evacuation, how are we to hear one another? We are in a metal tube with little oxygen already. What our company is spraying on the aircraft can be damaging to the human body.Neurologically speaking and hard to pinpoint.
1781104: I am not sure this is the correct plane or not as I forgot to write it up after my trip. I have a safety concern with the location of the survival kit lanyard on the OW (Over Water) aircraft. There is no way I would be able to attach the survival kit in a ditching as you can't get your hand back there to attach it as you can't get your hands that far back to get the lanyard. I would like to see a video of a Flight Attendant attaching the survival kit please, using a normal sized male flight attendant with the door closed. This move is putting crew and passengers at risk of not having the needed supplies in a ditching.
1781107: I took the insert of the food catered for the pilots up to the flight deck prior to passenger boarding. The Captain asked me to set it on the jump-seat behind him. During boarding, the Captain came out and told us that the First Officer does not wear a mask in the flight deck and asked if either Flight Attendant A or myself would be willing to come up to the flight deck if the Captain needed a lavatory break in flight. We both said that we would not be comfortable with coming up there if the First Officer was not wearing a mask. Upon landing, I realized that the insert of flight deck food remained in the flight deck until after landing.Better CRM between flight deck and flight attendants if this situation comes up. I honestly don't think that anyone even thought about it. Flight Attendant A and I just knew that we were not going to put ourselves into the flight deck if the First Officer wasn't wearing a mask, which we would have had to in order to grab the insert. But it absolutely was not intentionally left on the flight deck for takeoff and landing on our part.
1781109: Everything with arming the door at departure was fine. No issues with arming the door. Upon arrival, the girt bar was extremely difficult to place into the door bracket. When I was finally able to get it into the J-clips, I noticed that the bracket was too far to the left and would have caught on the fwd side of the aircraft door when opened by catering. I bent down and re-positioned the girt bar onto the J-clip, which was extremely difficult. It seems that the plastic collars on the girt bar need to be adjusted, the plastic collar on the right side is butted up against the slide flap, which makes it extremely difficult to place the girt into the clip. I asked the CA to look at it and explained my concern. He took the girt bar out of the J-clips and then placed the girt bar back into the J-clips, and also found it difficult to do so.Have Maintenance check the collars on the girt bar.
1781110: I was working the FWD cabin and Flight Attendant (FA) B was working the AFT. During the flight FA B approached the galley and states to me that she was going to give Passenger X a face mask warning, because he was having a hard time complying to keeping the mask over his nose and she asked on numerous occasions before pushback, taxing out to the runway, and during the flight to keep his mask over his nose. I called flight deck to inform the Captain what was about to happen. So FA B gave the written policy to Passenger X and he stated he didn't want to see it. FA B informs me what happened and I call the flight deck. I tell the Captain she gave the warning and Passenger X refuses to hear it. The Captain states we'll just call for supervisors to meet us at the gate. FA B and I both say 'okay.' I decide to do a walk through in the cabin and notice Passenger X has his mask on covering his nose and mouth. I inform FA B and the Captain. Captain states that's great, but so there's no further issues with Passenger X we'll still have the Supervisor meet us. I say 'fine.' I guess noticing that FA B and myself are talking to the Captain inflight, Passenger X states to FA B he now wants to read the policy. Once seeing the policy and reading it Passenger X states to FA B that he's sorry. FA B then calls the Captain to let him know Passenger X has a change of heart. Captain still states he'll have the Supervisor meet the aircraft at the gate. We say 'okay.' Once at the gate, I open the main door and the supervisors are there. They wait for Passenger X to deplane to talk to him. The supervisors also state they will inform his connecting flight.
1781112: On [Date] I was given the work assignment of running the #1 engine on Aircraft X for a BUG (Back-Up Generator) operational and leak check by my lead mechanic, ref log page. I knew that there was a fuel leak in the pylon for the #1 engine as I had written it up the day before, ref log page. At this time the left wing had 30,000 lbs of fuel in it to help find the leak source into the pylon. I declined to run the engine to verify the operation of the relatively minor repair of the BUG replacement compared to the danger of fire from an active fuel leak into the #1 engine's pylon. I explained my reasoning to the pair of shift foreman. They went away and returned with the directive to 'Run the Engine' regardless of the fuel leak or my concerns. The foreman said the Operating Manager had directed this. At this point I decided to run the engine as they ordered me to do rather than risk losing my job. I ran the engine with an eye for protecting my work partners and the aircraft as much as possible given the situation management forced me into. As the days have gone by since this happened it has bothered me more and more until I felt I had to reach out to the [Aviation Safety Action Program] and Ground Safety committees. Please take note of [Company] Engine Run Policy [Number].'At no time will safety be compromised for operational reasons'.
1781116: The pre-departure checklists have the following added to the header of the checklist: 'NOTE: This check is to be done at the gate or hangar prior to taking the aircraft to the gate at the discretion of the Lead or Supervisor. The purpose of this form is to guide technicians through the crew's pre-flight checks to improve our on-time departure rate.This form does not require documentation in [Company Documents] or the use of the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual). However, if a discrepancy is found as a result of this check, it must be documented.' This is clearly instructing maintenance personnel to perform maintenance activities without documentation in the aircraft paperwork system and is also stating that it is acceptable for maintenance personnel to perform maintenance activities without manual references. I believe this to be a violation of the federal aviation regulations and feel encouraging our workforce to perform any maintenance activities without documentation or proper manual references would diminish our safety and compliance culture.In order to have an acceptable pre-departure checklist per the [CFRs] (Code of Federal Regulations), an internal document should be added to AMM chapter X stating the checks to be performed and proper manual references, These checks should be properly documented as having been accomplished in our maintenance paperwork system.
1781139: At touchdown, aircraft started to pull right and right wing started to drop. I heard a noise and thought I had blown a tire. Next I flew back to centerline and in doing so I may have added slight power. I slapped the gear handle. I never heard a Gear Warning tone. When the Crew was asked, they said they didn't either.Settling down again, I kept the wings level and anticipated what I thought might be the inevitable right tendency.The aircraft however remained level, but I informed tower I had an issue and would roll out to the end. I appeared to have good control, and the noise was gone. I elected to taxi the short distance to the FBO with an escort of Airport Operations vehicles.By shutdown, all indications appeared to be normal again until post-flight inspection. At post-flight, damage was observed to the prop, the flap cowlings (subsequently the flap linkages), and rear avionics antennas.The approach to landing felt normal. I was sequenced between two aircraft and behind another Pilatus. Flaps were extended 7-8 miles from the airport and gear was extended on a final vector to the FAF approximately abeam the FAF. Landing checklist was completed via the IPAD, and a 'Last Finals' check was performed by myself at 500 foot call. (Last Finals: gear down-three green, flaps 15- final setting, lights on, landing clearance, go-around altitude set). Yaw Damper (YD) was disconnected at DH announcement.On GP for the ILS, Torque was normal at 6-7 inches with the AOA indicating middle or slightly lower. Idle power was set between 70-50 AGL. Initial touchdown was at TDZ or slightly beyond.ATC was typical for the airport and time of day.Maintenance and company management are investigating. And I have been reviewing my actions and performance in this event.
1781142: I was in contact with Chicago Center on our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on a direct flight plan at FL290. We were talking with Chicago Center when he transferred us to another Chicago Center frequency. I tried 3 times to contact the Controller as he was quite busy. The third time he said 'unless it is pertinent to the safety of flight, maintain radio silence.' I complied with his instructions.
